https://www.politico.eu/article/eurovisi.text: Eurovision has changed its rules to block countries involved in armed conflict or any other “sensitive geopolitical situation” from hosting the annual song contest. The change comes as the last two years of the contest have been overshadowed by controversy surrounding Israel’s participation. Five countries staged an unprecedented boycott of the 2026 contest rather than compete alongside Israel. They pointed to the country’s war in Gaza — sparked by the October 2023 attack on Israel by Hamas militants — and the resulting humanitarian crisis it triggered. Advertisement Advertisement Despite this, Israel has come close to winning the 2025 and 2026 editions of the competition, garnering a strong public vote. Israel’s pubic broadcaster KAN has denied claims that results were unfairly influenced by mass voting campaigns. Eurovision is organized by the European Broadcasting Union, an alliance of 113 public service media organizations across 56 countries. Typically, the national broadcaster that wins the competition hosts the following edition in their home country. There have been some exceptions. When Ukraine won the 2022 contest, the organizers said the country could not host the following year’s contest due to Russia’s ongoing invasion raising safety concerns. The new rules would make a winning broadcaster automatically ineligible to host “if an armed conflict, a sensitive geopolitical situation, or any other situation materially affects the security, safety or stability of their state or immediate region.” The organizers could still commission an independent security assessment to determine whether a winner can safely host the contest. If a winner is deemed unable to host, the broadcasting union has the power to choose an alternative. Organizers said the rule change follows “feedback from participating broadcasters” after the 2026 contest in Vienna. They will apply from next year, when the contest takes place in Bulgaria. “These changes are about giving everyone involved greater clarity, protecting artists and ensuring the Contest continues to provide a safe and welcoming environment, while preserving the spirit and integrity that make the Eurovision Song Contest so special,” said Eurovision director Martin Green. Vijayan Trishul Defence Solutions signs tech pact with Czech firm DEUS Automation The agreement represents one of the first major technology-transfer collaborations in the small-calibre ammunition sector between the two countries By BL Mumbai Bureau Updated - August 09, 2026 at 11:14 AM. | Mumbai × Share WhatsApp X Facebook LinkedIn Messenger Reddit Mail https://www.thehindubusinessline.com/news/vijayan-trishul-defence-solutions-signs-tech-pact-with-czech-firm-deus-automation/article71324094.ece Copy Vijayan Trishul Defence Solutions, the Ministry of Home Affairs licensed manufacturer of small arms and ammunition, has entered into a strategic technology partnership with DEUS Automation a.s., a sister company of the STV Group of the Czech Republic. The agreement represents one of the first major technology-transfer collaborations in the small-calibre ammunition sector between the two countries. Through this collaboration, VTDS will gain access to advanced international manufacturing technologies and expertise that will contribute to the development of modern ammunition production capabilities in India. Founded by Sahil Luthra, Managing Director and Prikansha Luthra, Director, VTDS has emerged as a forward-looking Indian defence enterprise focused on advancing indigenous capabilities in the small arms and ammunition domain. Under the agreement, DEUS Automation will provide advanced manufacturing technology for the production of small-calibre ammunition in India. The technology transfer will enable VTDS to establish manufacturing capabilities built on international quality benchmarks, precision engineering standards, and modern production systems, creating a strong foundation for future growth and technological advancement. Sahil Luthra said that by working with DEUS Automation, the company will take a meaningful step towards building modern manufacturing capabilities in India while contributing to the nation’s long-term defence preparedness and industrial self-reliance. Prikansha Luthra said the collaboration is not only about technology transfer but also about building a sustainable ecosystem of innovation, manufacturing excellence and strategic capability. “We believe partnerships of this nature will play an important role in strengthening India’s defence manufacturing landscape and creating enduring industrial value for the future,” she said. Representing DEUS Automation, Alex Cerny, CEO and Member of the Board and Ondrej Cerny, Manager of Sales, Projects & Purchase, noted that the agreement reflects a shared vision of supporting India’s expanding defence manufacturing ambitions through the transfer of proven international expertise and production technologies. Beyond its immediate manufacturing objectives, the alliance establishes a framework for sustained cooperation between Indian and Czech defence industries in the areas of technology exchange, industrial development, and future innovation. https://www.trend.az/casia/kazakhstan/42.text: Home Central Asia Kazakhstan Kazakhstan and Central African Republic establish diplomatic relations Kazakhstan News 23 September 2026 16:25 (UTC +04:00) Photo: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Kazakhstan Alyona Pavlenko Read more BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 23. Kazakhstan and the Central African Republic have established diplomatic relations, Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said. The agreement was reached on the first day of the High-Level Week of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly in New York, where Kazakhstan’s Foreign Minister Mukhtar Tleuberdi held a series of bilateral meetings and took part in multilateral events. “An important outcome of the first day was the establishment of diplomatic relations between the Republic of Kazakhstan and the Central African Republic. The heads of the foreign ministries of the two countries signed the relevant Joint Communiqué, confirming their mutual interest in developing bilateral ties and cooperation on international platforms,” the ministry said. Tleuberdi also held talks with the foreign ministers of Hungary Anita Orban, Moldova Mihai Popșoi, Poland Radosław Sikorski, Slovenia Tanja Fajon, Ukraine Andrii Sybiha and El Salvador Alexandra Hill Tinoco. The meetings addressed current issues of bilateral cooperation, prospects for expanding political dialogue and trade and economic ties, as well as an exchange of views on key international and regional issues. Separate meetings were held with UN Trade and Development Secretary-General and candidate for UN Secretary-General Rebeca Grynspan and UNESCO Director-General Khaled El-Enany. The sides discussed strengthening multilateral cooperation, improving the effectiveness of international institutions and further cooperation between Kazakhstan and UN system organizations. As part of the multilateral program, Kazakhstan’s foreign minister also participated in the ministerial meeting “Renewal and Focus: The UN We Need 5 Years from Now,” dedicated to the prospects for the development of the UN and its adaptation to current global challenges. https://www.dw.com/en/german-national-fa.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5Ocsy The public prosecutor general (Generalbundesanwalt beim Bundesgerichtshof) is the federal prosecutor of Germany (File: 2019) Image: Christoph Schmidt/dpa/picture alliance Advertisement Germany 's prosecutor's office said that a German national has been placed in pre-trial detention for allegedly attempting to join the so-called "Islamic State" terror group , while abroad, German news agency dpa reported. What is known about the case The agency cited a spokeswoman for the Federal Prosecutor's Office as saying that an arrest warrant had been executed and that a 21-year-old was extradited to Germany. The suspect is accused of travelling to Ethiopia from Berlin in January 2025, with the purpose of joining the IS terror group in Somalia. Prosecutors allege that he never reached Somalia , but instead traveled to Pakistan to join IS, where he was reportedly arrested in February 2025. The suspect stands accused of attempted membership in a terrorist organization abroad. He is also accused of preparing a serious act of violence endangering the state. Germany and the so-called "Islamic State" Islamic extremists have carried out several attacks in Germany over the years. The deadliest was when a truck rammed a Berlin Christmas market in 2016, killing 12 people. In July a German court sentenced a man and a woman to lengthy prison sentences for enslaving and abusing two Yazidi girls under the so-called "Islamic State" group in Iraq. The Iraqi couple was convicted of war crimes, genocide and crimes against humanity. They were also convicted of sexually abusing children and aiding and abetting the listed offenses. The couple, identified as Twana H.S. and Asia R.A., in line with German privacy laws, were most recently living in Germany and were arrested in the southern state of Bavaria in April in 2024. Photograph: Charly Triballeau/AFP/Getty Images Jared Kushner New book makes fiery claims about Jared Kushner’s finances in Trump’s first term Kushner threatens to sue, denying allegations that two slush funds were set up to influence his Middle East role Martin Pengelly Wed 28 Oct 2026 17.56 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A new book containing incendiary claims about Jared Kushner ’s financial dealings during Donald Trump ’s first term has ignited a political and media firestorm. The book by author Matthew Cole is called Princes and Thieves: Jared Kushner and Mohamed bin Zayed’s Secret Plot to Remake the Middle East and was released in the US this week. An excerpt was published by Vanity Fair last Thursday, and immediately drew a furious response from Kushner, who called its claims “completely insane”. The book contains numerous allegations about Kushner, whose father-in-law is Trump and who has served as one of his top diplomatic envoys in the Middle East – the most explosive of which are claims linking him to huge bank accounts allegedly funded by Gulf states. Kusher denounced the book on his site last week, and writing on X : “We denied every one of these claims on the record, yet the author failed to provide a single shred of evidence to substantiate any of them.” He has demanded that Vanity Fair retract the excerpt and has threatened legal action against the book’s publisher, Simon & Schuster. He added: “During the period in question, I was one of the most scrutinized people in the world, subjected to intense media coverage, multiple congressional investigations, and a special counsel investigation. I voluntarily cooperated with these investigations, providing over 30 hours of testimony. None of these allegations ever surfaced, because none of these events ever happened.” The Guardian contacted Kushner’s legal counsel from Clare Locke as well as Chad Mizelle for comment and received no response. Cole’s sources are predominantly anonymous and he does not print images of emails or other documentation to support his reporting. Extensive footnotes indicate sources of information, including confidential interviews. In the book, the top intelligence official in the United Arab Emirates, Ali Al Shamsi, is reported to have called Kushner “the most expensive employee we’ve ever had”. The book details alleged payments into two “slush fund” bank accounts allegedly set up for Kushner by Emirati prince Mohamed bin Zayed (MBZ) and Saudi Arabian prince Mohammed bin Salman (MBS) during Trump’s first term. The Guardian contacted the Saudi Arabian and Emirati embassies for comment and did not receive a response. In the book, Cole claims the accounts were partially managed by Kushner on an iPhone hacked by Russian and Dutch intelligence. But despite the Emirati spymaster’s opinion of Kushner, Cole alleges that the New Jersey real estate scion was not entirely trusted. Cole describes a dangerous world in which blackmail is as common a tool of statecraft as torture and murder, as in the cases of the Saudi journalist Jamal Khashoggi, killed on the orders of MBS in Turkey in 2018, and the Emirati journalist and poet Habib Al Sayegh , whose killing by agents of MBZ in 2019 is described by Cole. Kushner continues to steer US foreign policy despite having no official role, with questions about his business interests accompanying him as he travels the world with New York real estate magnate Steve Witkoff, this week seeking peace in Ukraine, if on terms favorable to Russia. In response, an attorney “who has represented President Trump in multiple defamation lawsuits”, Alejandro Brito, told Cole that, “during his time working for President Trump, Kushner ‘always represented and sought the interests of the United States and the President of the United States and did not make any agreements or arrangements with leaders or officials in foreign countries that were not agreed by the President of the United States and in the best interests of the United States.’” He further said that “[a]ny allegation that Kushner knew of, had access to, had authorization for or engaged in or directed any conduct related to any government-funded or government-linked bank account is totally false and defamatory”. Brito told Cole that “‘there are no accounts and never were.’” Cole writes that the Dutch government refused to comment in response to his questions about the alleged hacking of Kushner’s phone. According to Cole, MBZ and MBS wanted Kushner to help achieve their “vision of a new Middle East, one in which Israel would become an integral part of the region, recognized diplomatically by Gulf Arabs today and eventually by the rest of the Arab world; the Palestinians would end their conflict with Israel and accept a peace built on prosperity; Islamic extremism would be defeated; and Iran’s expansionism and militancy would retreat, either by persuasion or force.” Nearly 10 years later, the US and Israel are planning new strikes in their eight-month war with Iran; Saudi Arabia is at war with Houthi rebels in Yemen, and Israel has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians in Gaza since the Hamas attacks of 7 October 2023. Kushner entered Trump’s first administration with his wife, Ivanka Trump, as close presidential advisers. MBZ and MBS, Cole claims, saw a chance to secure the best access money could buy. Cole alleges that in early 2017 the two princes “proposed to give Kushner a fund, a bank account, which the two leaders, working with Jared, would use to identify and pay for projects and foreign policy goals to advance for President Trump’s benefit”. According to Cole, an idea to fund Trump’s proposed wall on the US border with Mexico apparently did not work out but the author claims that “MBZ and MBS initially, and then MBZ alone, put at least $2bn into at least two banks for Kushner.” Classifying the accounts as “Alpha” and “Beta”, Cole claims the Alpha account was held at First Abu Dhabi Bank, the largest in UAE, and contained “roughly $750m” to be “used as a foreign policy fund” overseen by Kushner and MBZ and meant to help end the Israel-Palestine conflict. Cole quotes a source who says he knew of the UAE’s alleged deal with Kushner as saying: “‘Jared was looking for shortcuts in his diplomacy.’” Cole writes: “This person held discussions with both senior UAE and Israeli officials about the secret financial arrangement between Kushner, the UAE, and, at least initially, Saudi Arabia. ‘Jared promised MBZ that he’d push their agenda with Trump if they participated in a fund. He wanted normalization with Israel so that business could take off,’” the source alleged. The same source claimed that “a slush fund – a shared pool of money for off-the-books diplomatic objectives – was a common form of Gulf Arab government corruption … ‘The Emiratis and the Saudis do this once a year. A billion or two is nothing for them, and if it gets them what they want, it’s money well spent.’” Citing “a person briefed on the Beta account”, Cole claims it contained “roughly $1bn” and at the suggestion of the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, was moved by MBZ to the Israeli Central Bank via Azerbaijan, a favored conduit for laundering money. “It is … unclear how Kushner used the money the UAE deposited into the Beta account for him,” Cole alleges, “but according to the person with knowledge of the money, its allocation was for Kushner’s personal benefit.” Kushner’s attorney, Brito, told Cole his client “had no financial relationships with any foreign countries or leaders”, adding that his “complete financial disclosures are publicly available in his OGE [office of government ethics] form 278e filings during this period.” Cole alleges that the “Alpha” account established for Kushner in Trump’s first term was drained by failed schemes and Kushner’s access was cut off. “It is unclear if the Israeli government allowed Kushner access to the Beta bank account” after the end of Trump’s first term, Cole writes. Cole also examines the widely reported story about how Kushner ultimately secured Qatari investment in 666 Fifth Avenue, a marquee Manhattan property, thereby profiting from interests on both sides of a bitterly divided Middle East, given Saudi Arabia and UAE’s rivalry with Qatar. (Kushner has denied engaging in any conflicts of interest.) In Trump’s second term, Kushner’s diplomatic work has been dogged by questions about another massive financial asset: a $2bn investment by the Saudi sovereign wealth fund in Kushner’s Affinity Partners private equity firm, made after Trump left power in 2021. Cole quotes an unnamed Arab official and Affinity investor who claimed: “We don’t pay Jared because he’s a savvy investor. We pay him to keep him happy. That keeps his father-in-law happy.” Cole writes: “Deep relationships with MBZ, MBS, Emir Al Thani [of Qatar], and Bibi Netanyahu were useful as [Kushner] shuttled between capitals, trying to find a way to end the daily slaughter in Gaza. But as it had been when he was a government employee, there was little record of what his investors were negotiating with him.” In his epilogue, Cole writes that Kushner “declined multiple requests for an on-the-record interview for the book”, adding that he “first contacted him with a list of questions in May 2026 and followed up via email twice more, asking additional questions.” Through his lawyers, Kushner denounced all of Cole’s reporting. Also on X, Chad Mizelle, a Trump administration lawyer who identified himself as “Jared’s attorney”, said : “The central allegation in this book is categorically false. These are not questions of interpretation or competing recollections: there are no bank accounts. They don’t exist. These are egregious and defamatory claims without a shred of evidence to substantiate them.” Explore more on these topics Jared Kushner Trump administration US politics Middle East and north Africa US foreign policy news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness
